qs.q: A 52-year-old woman with early menopause and troublesome menopausal symptoms is considered for hormone replacement therapy (HRT). What is the primary indication for HRT in this patient?
o: Prevention of metastatic bone disease progression in postmenopausal women
Prevention of osteoporosis and treatment of menopausal symptoms in early menopause
First-line long-term maintenance in older women with established osteoporosis
Permanent suppression of osteoblastic activity in patients with bone loss
qs.e: HRT is primarily indicated for the prevention of osteoporosis in women with an early menopause and for treatment of women with osteoporosis in their early fifties who have troublesome menopausal symptoms. It should be avoided in older women with established osteoporosis due to risks of breast cancer and cardiovascular disease.

qs.q: A 55-year-old postmenopausal woman discusses long-term options for fracture prevention. Why is hormone replacement therapy no longer recommended as a first-line approach for treating osteoporosis?
o: It interferes with the intestinal cellular uptake of dietary calcium and vitamin D
It acts primarily as a bone-softening agent that leads to osteomalacia-like changes
It directly stimulates osteoclast activity via the suppression of endogenous calcitonin
It has been linked to an increased risk for breast cancer and venous thromboembolism
qs.e: Estrogen-progestin therapy is no longer considered first-line because it has been linked to an increased risk for breast cancer, stroke, venous thromboembolism, and coronary disease. Estrogen is now recommended primarily if patients seek relief of postmenopausal symptoms.

qs.q: Which disease of bone is managed using hormone replacement therapy to counteract decreased bone mass?
qs.e: Osteoporosis features significant decreases in bone mass and is commonly treated with bisphosphonates and hormone replacement therapy. Paget's disease involves disorganized bone remodeling rather than standard postmenopausal bone loss.

exam: A 52‑year‑old woman presents with fatigue and weight gain. What is the first test you order? — TSH to screen for hypothyroidism, then free T4 if TSH abnormal.
A patient on hydrocortisone develops hyperglycaemia. What is the next step? — Reduce hydrocortisone dose, add insulin if needed, monitor glucose.

A man with low libido is found to have low testosterone. Why is testosterone replacement preferred over estrogen? — Testosterone restores libido and muscle mass; estrogen would worsen cardiovascular risk.
A post‑thyroidectomy patient has a TSH of 12 mIU/L. What is the therapeutic target? — TSH 0.5–2.5 mIU/L with symptom relief.
A patient with chronic kidney disease needs levothyroxine. Why is dose adjustment necessary? — Reduced clearance of thyroid hormone; start lower and titrate slowly.
A patient with HIV is on antiretroviral therapy and develops fatigue. What hormone deficiency should you consider? — Adrenal insufficiency due to TB or drug interactions.
ai.title: Hormone Replacement Therapy
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Hormone replacement therapy (HRT) restores deficient hormones, improves symptoms, and prevents complications. In low‑resource settings, focus on clinical diagnosis, affordable tests, and safe, generic medications.

sections.p: HRT is the administration of hormones to replace those that are deficient or absent, aiming to restore normal physiology and prevent disease progression.

b: Hypothyroidism: TSH >10 mIU/L or overt symptoms
Adrenal insufficiency: ACTH stimulation test showing inadequate cortisol rise
sections.p: Severity is graded by clinical symptoms and laboratory values, guiding dose titration and monitoring.
Common causes in East Africa include iodine deficiency, tuberculosis, HIV‑related adrenal disease, and post‑surgical thyroidectomy.

b: Hypothyroidism: cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin
sections.p: Symptoms mirror the deficient hormone: fatigue, weight loss, cold intolerance, skin changes, menstrual irregularities, or sexual dysfunction.
Use affordable, point‑of‑care tests where possible; interpret results in clinical context.

t.b: TSH >10 mIU/L or >5 mIU/L with low free T4 indicates hypothyroidism
Baseline <5 µg/dL or inadequate rise after ACTH stimulation
Large goiter or nodules suggest iodine deficiency or malignancy

sections.p: Watch for acute adrenal crisis, thyroid storm, or hormone excess symptoms.

b: Levothyroxine – start low, increase to TSH 0.5‑2.5 mIU/L
sections.p: Treat the underlying cause, then start replacement with the safest, most affordable drug, titrating to symptom control and lab targets.

t.b: Begin 5 µg/kg/day or 50–75 µg/day in adults, adjust based on TSH
After confirming low total testosterone and symptoms of hypogonadism

b: TSH every 6–12 months after stable dose
sections.p: Regular review of symptoms, weight, blood pressure, and labs; counsel on iodine intake and infection prevention.
Other endocrine disorders can mimic HRT deficiency.
Low iodine intake can give normal TSH but low free T4; ACTH stimulation may be falsely normal in early adrenal disease.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe hypotension, confusion, vomiting, or inability to take oral medication (possible adrenal crisis)
